Tundra

/TUN-druh/ — sounds like TUN-duh · noun

Hear It

What It Means

The tundra is a vast, flat, treeless region, typically in the Arctic, where the ground beneath the surface usually stays frozen year-round.

Nothing taller than a shrub grows on the windswept tundra.

Worked Example

The Arctic explorer stepped onto the tundra and gasped—in every direction, nothing but low shrubs and frozen ground stretched endlessly to the horizon.

Tundra is more precise than 'frozen wasteland' or 'Arctic region' because it specifically describes a biome defined by permafrost, treelessness, and minimal vegetation—not just any cold place.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

frozen wasteland: A frozen wasteland is any cold, empty land where almost nothing seems to survive — the phrase paints how a place looks and feels, not what it is. Tundra names a real, exactly defined biome: treeless land over permanently frozen soil, quietly alive with mosses and hardy low shrubs.

arctic region: An arctic region is simply a far-northern part of the world, located by latitude, and it can hold glaciers, open ocean, or forest. Tundra is defined by conditions instead of address: treeless land on permanently frozen ground, whether it lies in the Arctic or high on a mountain.

permafrost zone: A permafrost zone is any area where the ground below the surface stays frozen all year, no matter what grows on top of it. Tundra adds the surface picture: a flat, treeless biome of mosses and low shrubs living above that permanently frozen ground.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

forest: a large area thickly covered with trees

rainforest: a hot, wet forest dense with plant life

Where it sits · how little plant life it supports — rainforest → grassland → shrubland → tundra

rainforest vs. tundra: A rainforest is the lushest, most plant-packed biome, the very opposite of the tundra, which is so cold and barren that trees cannot grow there at all.

grassland vs. tundra: A grassland supports far more life than the tundra, since it is covered in grasses and grazing herds, while the frozen tundra allows only low, hardy plants.

shrubland vs. tundra: Shrubland is closer to the tundra but still greener: it grows woody bushes, whereas the tundra's frozen ground keeps vegetation down to mosses and tiny shrubs.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — tundra

Root — tundra: treeless, elevated wasteland; marshy Arctic plain (Russian (from Sami/Lappish 'tundar'))

Put it together

Put it together: Tundra was borrowed whole from Russian, which took it from the Sami word 'tundar' meaning a treeless, elevated wasteland — exactly the cold, barren, frozen plain the word names today.

Use the root in a new word: taiga

Use the root in a new word: taiga: Tundra has no English root relatives — it was borrowed whole from Russian, which took it from the Sami word for a treeless plain. English picked up taiga, the great northern forest that borders the tundra, the very same way: two lone Arctic loanwords, each standing on its own rather than belonging to a word family.

Strength Check

Word Choice

scientific / geographic

Use tundra specifically when describing Arctic and high-altitude treeless biomes. Don't confuse it with vague terms like 'wasteland' or 'frozen land.' Tundra names a particular ecosystem defined by permafrost, extreme cold, and the absence of trees.
